passage: By the school slide, "Come on, join the line," said Karthik. "It's too long," said Jagdish. "There are ten kids." "It moves fast." "I don't want to play anyway." "You said you wanted the slide all morning." "It's a baby game." Jagdish kicked a stone toward the corner. "I'm going to sit there." Karthik shrugged and joined the line. He went down twice. From the corner Jagdish picked at the wall and said to nobody, "It's boring."

qa.q: Where did Jagdish go instead of joining the line?
qa.a: Jagdish went to sit in the corner.

qa.q: What might Jagdish really be feeling when he says, "I don't want to play anyway"?
qa.a: Jagdish may be disappointed and tired of the long line, and covering it up by acting as if nothing matters. Watching from the corner and calling it boring hint at that.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try instead, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish could ask Karthik to save a place, or count the children and wait. Waiting gets the slide that was wanted all morning.

qa.q: How does the moment look to Karthik?
qa.a: Karthik offered help and sees Jagdish walk away from the slide that was wanted all morning. Karthik may be puzzled and shrug it off.

grounding: A child walks away from a long slide line saying the game does not matter, which protects feelings but gets no turn.

passage:
Note for Kunal's parents
At recess today the swing line was long. Kunal stood in it for a moment, then walked to the corner by the water tank and said loudly, "I don't want to play anyway." He sat with his back to the swings. I noticed he watched the swings over his shoulder. I asked if he'd like to join the line with me, and we waited together.

qa.a: To the corner by the water tank.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he said "I don't want to play anyway"?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and impatient, pretending not to care to hide it.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do, and why might it help?
qa.a: They offered to wait in line with him, which made the waiting feel easier and got him a turn.

qa.q: How might Kunal's parents feel reading this?
qa.a: They might feel sympathetic and glad someone noticed his feelings behind the words.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child who walks off from a long line saying he doesn't want to play, protecting his feelings and missing his turn.

passage: At the temple fair in Sirsi, the line for the toy train went round the banyan tree. Akash looked at it, kicked a stone and said to his sister Nikita, "I don't even want to go. It's a baby ride." He sat down on the steps. Nikita stayed in line. When she rode past, waving, Akash watched every round, chin on his hands.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as he watched every round?
qa.a: He was disappointed and wistful, wishing he'd stayed in line.

qa.q: What would you advise Akash next time?
qa.a: Stay in line with Nikita and talk while waiting, because giving up means missing the ride.

qa.q: How might Nikita see Akash on the steps?
qa.a: Nikita might feel a bit sorry for him and guess he really wanted the ride.

grounding: A child walks away from a long line saying he doesn't want to go, which protects his feelings but costs him a turn.
